WHAT’S HAPPENING

“Look at your face, Lorraine.”

He said it on his way out the door. So Lorraine, 61, did the only thing she knew how to do: up at 5:30, walking until her legs gave out. No wine. No bread. No sugar. The weight started coming off. Her belt went in a notch.

Her face didn’t get the message. Her daughter finally said it out loud: “You look thinner, and you look worse. You’ve gone puffy and gray.”

WHAT’S REALLY GOING ON

Your insulin still works. Your cells stopped answering it.

When you eat, sugar moves into your blood, and insulin knocks on your cells to let it in so they can turn it into energy. After years of stress, short nights and grabbing whatever’s fast, the cells stop answering the way they used to.

So the sugar lingers, your cells run short on fuel, and you feel it: the 3 p.m. fog, the pull toward the pantry at night, and a body that looks worn out no matter how many miles you walk.

No wine, no bread, no sugar?

Crashing every afternoon?

4

Mistake: Blaming your willpower

The 3 p.m. slump and the 11 p.m. pantry trip aren’t a character flaw. When your cells aren’t taking in fuel, they’re running on empty in a bloodstream full of it, and they send you looking for more.

Instead: Berberine HCl (500 mg) supports cellular energy production and healthy glucose metabolism.†

Grabbing cinnamon from the grocery store?

5

Mistake: Thinking all cinnamon is the same

Most cinnamon sold in America is cassia, a different tree. Go look in your cupboard: one thick, hard roll of bark is cassia. True Ceylon is thin and papery, with layers rolled inside each other. Cassia is so high in a compound called coumarin that Europe limits how much can go into food.

Instead: Choose true Ceylon. Resilia uses Ceylon cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum) bark extract, never cassia.†
